diagnosis: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL), not otherwise specified (NOS), germinal-center B-cell-like (GCB) immunophenotype by the Hans algorithm (CD10 diffuse positive, BCL6 positive, MUM1/IRF4 negative; BCL2 ~30%, MYC ~20%, Ki-67 ~70%; EBER negative), with no MYC, BCL2 or BCL6 rearrangement on FISH (not double-hit/triple-hit and not a double-expressor by IHC). Diagnosed on CT-guided core biopsy of the retroperitoneal mass; bone marrow morphology, immunohistochemistry and flow cytometry are negative for lymphoma.
stage: Ann Arbor stage IVB: large (9.4 cm) FDG-avid retroperitoneal/mesenteric conglomerate nodal mass plus extranodal involvement of the right kidney (3.2 cm), left adrenal gland (2.6 cm) and liver segment VI (1.8 cm), with B symptoms (drenching night sweats, 8 kg/10% weight loss). No supradiaphragmatic, bone marrow, testicular or documented CNS involvement. IPI 5 of 5 (age >60, stage IV, LDH > ULN, >1 extranodal site, ECOG 2); CNS-IPI 6 of 6.
biology: GCB DLBCL with high proliferation (Ki-67 ~70%) but favorable molecular features: no MYC/BCL2/BCL6 rearrangement and no double-expressor phenotype (MYC 20%, BCL2 30%), EBER negative. This argues against high-grade B-cell lymphoma with double-hit/triple-hit biology. The main biologic uncertainty is that the right renal, left adrenal and liver lesions were not biopsied; their intense, concordant FDG avidity makes lymphoma most likely, but a synchronous renal cell carcinoma (with adrenal/liver metastases) has not been excluded histologically.
prognosis: Potentially curable, but high risk. IPI 5 predicts roughly 30% 5-year PFS/OS with R-CHOP-type therapy, with improvement expected from Pola-R-CHP; GCB subtype and absence of double-hit features are favorable. CNS-IPI 6 predicts a high risk of CNS relapse (on the order of 10-15% at 2 years), particularly given renal and adrenal involvement. The markedly elevated LDH (1,290 U/L), large tumor burden, B symptoms, declining renal function (eGFR 50) and high tumor-lysis risk make the next few weeks precarious; response to first-line therapy will be the dominant determinant of outcome.
first_line_treatment: Start curative-intent systemic therapy promptly, within days, after tumor-lysis precautions. My regimen is Pola-R-CHP (polatuzumab vedotin plus rituximab, cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, prednisone) every 21 days for 6 cycles, with full-dose doxorubicin (baseline LVEF 60%) and pegfilgrastim primary prophylaxis. This is a category 1 NCCN regimen for advanced-stage DLBCL with IPI >=2 and offers a PFS advantage over R-CHOP; if polatuzumab is not available or approved, R-CHOP x6 is the appropriate equivalent. I would not use DA-EPOCH-R or a reduced-intensity/frailty regimen: there is no double-hit disease and his ECOG 2 is largely disease-related, so he should be treated with curative intent. I would not add consolidative radiation up front; reserve involved-site radiation for residual PET-positive or bulky residual disease after chemotherapy.
cns_risk: High: CNS-IPI 6 of 6 (age >60, stage IV, ECOG 2, elevated LDH, >1 extranodal site, and kidney/adrenal involvement), although he has no neurological symptoms. I will obtain baseline CSF cytology and flow cytometry (and MRI brain only if symptoms develop). If the CSF is negative, I will give CNS prophylaxis with intrathecal methotrexate (4 doses during the first cycles) because high-dose intravenous methotrexate is not safe with eGFR 50. I recognize that the evidence for intrathecal prophylaxis is weak and that it mainly addresses leptomeningeal rather than parenchymal relapse; if renal function recovers to normal, high-dose systemic methotrexate would be the preferred prophylaxis. A positive CSF or new neurological findings would change the plan to CNS-directed therapy.
response_assessment: Baseline PET-CT is complete. Do not change treatment based on an interim PET outside a trial. Assess response with PET-CT using Lugano 2014/Deauville criteria about 6-8 weeks after cycle 6 (no later than 12 weeks), together with repeat CT, LDH, CBC and renal function. Deauville 1-3 is a complete metabolic response. Because the baseline mass is large, a residual non-FDG-avid mass may be fibrosis. If Deauville 4-5, biopsy the residual site (including the renal/adrenal/liver lesions to exclude a second malignancy) and either give involved-site radiation for limited residual disease or proceed to second-line salvage therapy and CAR-T if truly refractory. Progressive disease at any point or a rising LDH would prompt restaging and a change of therapy.
pretreatment_workup: Already completed and adequate: CBC with differential, CMP, LDH, uric acid, beta-2 microglobulin, HIV, HBV (HBsAg negative, anti-HBc negative, anti-HBs reactive, so no HBV antiviral prophylaxis is needed), HCV, PET-CT, echocardiogram (LVEF 60%), bone marrow aspirate/biopsy (negative), and MYC/BCL2/BCL6 FISH. Before cycle 1 I still need: G6PD level (mandatory before rasburicase), repeat electrolytes/creatinine/uric acid and urinalysis, baseline CSF as above, dental evaluation, and documentation of baseline neuropathy and cardiac risk. I will give inactivated influenza, COVID-19 and pneumococcal vaccines before rituximab if not current (live vaccines are contraindicated), and will not delay lymphoma treatment for them. I would not routinely biopsy the renal/adrenal/liver lesions before starting therapy, but I will reassess them on the end-of-treatment PET.
supportive_care: Tumor lysis is the immediate danger: large tumor burden, LDH 1,290, uric acid 10.4, renal involvement and eGFR 50 place him at high risk. For cycle 1, admit or closely observe with vigorous IV hydration and frequent potassium, phosphorus, calcium, uric acid and creatinine monitoring; give rasburicase 0.2 mg/kg after confirming G6PD status (use allopurinol with hydration if G6PD deficient), then allopurinol. Stop ibuprofen now: it is contributing to the AKI and is unsafe with this renal/TLS risk; use acetaminophen (with a daily maximum) and short-acting opioids for the abdominal pain. Give pegfilgrastim, 5-HT3-based antiemetics plus dexamethasone (consider olanzapine), and monitor glucose closely because steroids will worsen his diabetes; hold metformin if renal function worsens. Reserve PJP prophylaxis for prolonged/high-dose steroids (sulfa allergy: use atovaquone or pentamidine). Use VTE prophylaxis if hospitalized, encourage mobility, and involve nephrology if creatinine rises. Provide nutrition/social-work support, coordinate local labs/telehealth for the 45-minute commute, avoid live vaccines, and counsel on infection precautions and gout prophylaxis.
fitness_and_goals: ECOG 2, age 67, with T2DM, hypertension, gout and CKD, but he is independent in self-care, has normal LVEF and is highly motivated; his fatigue is largely disease-related. He is fit for full-dose anthracycline-based curative therapy, and he explicitly wants cure. His personal goal is attending his granddaughter's wedding in mid-December, so I will schedule the 21-day cycles to keep the expected nadir away from that week and use growth factor support, while explaining that treatment should not be delayed given the bulky, high-LDH disease and declining renal function. If he becomes truly frail or develops significant organ dysfunction, I would reassess and consider a reduced-intensity approach, but that is not the current plan. Early advance-care-planning discussions and involvement of his wife and daughter are appropriate.

Cause of the declining renal function (NSAID nephrotoxicity vs tumor infiltration/TLS) and urinalysis
Availability and insurance approval of polatuzumab vedotin
Baseline dental evaluation and varicella-zoster IgG
Prior vaccination history and quantitative immunoglobulins
Formal frailty/geriatric assessment and baseline neuropathy assessment
Patient's preference regarding intrathecal CNS prophylaxis and tolerance of extra procedures
Prior imaging for the 4 mm right upper lobe pulmonary nodule
Advance care planning and health-care proxy documentation
Whether the patient can reliably travel for 6 cycles and who will monitor glucose and renal function locally
